captions.text: Recap of chapter 06: you wrote a chat function, and sent messages with roles.
A system message sets the rules for the conversation.
Streaming gives you a reply piece by piece.
And two puzzles: the answers changed, and the model forgot your name.
Today's black box: the AI model itself.
Let's open it.

scenes.title: An LLM has one job: predict what comes next
flow: Give each next token a chance

captions.text: First, it reads all the text so far.
It gives every possible next token a chance.
It picks one token.
It adds that token, and repeats. This loop writes the whole reply.
These experiments use your chat function, plus two measuring tools provided for you.
You don't need to memorize these. They ask Ollama to report what the model did.
This one asks for the model's top guesses for the next token.
Experiment 1. These are the inputs: five pieces of text.
For each one, we print its characters and its tokens. Tokens are small chunks of text.
Predict: which of these five texts will take the most tokens?
Here's the output. Unusual words and numbers take more tokens.
Other languages often take more too. Limits and costs are counted in tokens.
Experiment 2. The input is an unfinished sentence: The capital of France is.
Predict: how sure will the model be about the next word?
The output shows the model's top guesses for the next token, with their chances.
The blanks probably reflect quiz-style text it saw in training. It predicts text. It doesn't look up facts.
Experiment 3. The input is one prompt, asking for a coffee shop name.
We ask six times at each temperature: 0, 0.7 and 1.5.
Predict: how many different names will each temperature give?
At 0, the model always takes the top choice, so all six names match.
That solves puzzle 1. The default temperature isn't 0, so answers vary.
Experiment 4. First we say: My name is Asha. Then we ask: What is my name?
Predict: will the separate call know the name?
The separate call sends only the question. Each call starts from nothing, so it fails.
That solves puzzle 2. Send the earlier messages, and it knows the name.
Experiment 5. The input hides a secret code at the start of a long message.
We ask for the code twice, using a large context window and a small one.
Predict: will the small window still find the code?
The large window finds it. With the small one, the code was lost, and there was no error.
Experiment 6. The input asks for a summary of a paper that doesn't exist.
Predict: will the model admit the paper isn't real?
The model summarized it confidently. This is called hallucination.
That's a big reason why agents need tools.
Your turn. Open exercises.py and complete the five TODOs.
You've finished when you see 5 passed.
